title: Tech Edition
dek: Xbox 360 recompilation is turning Blue Dragon into a native PC game, obsolete film scanners are gaining a hardware-verified public protocol reference, and agent-memory research is shifting from ‘can it store this?’ to ‘can it still use it later?’

lead_stories.headline: Blue Dragon is escaping the Xbox 360 through static recompilation
lead_stories.summary: re:Blue 1.0 rebuilds Blue Dragon as a native Windows, Linux and macOS application using the ReXGlue Xbox 360 recompilation toolkit. It supports modern resolutions, unlocked frame rates, native keyboard and mouse, Steam Deck, profiles and a built-in mod manager while requiring the user’s own three retail discs.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: This is a useful midpoint between emulation and full source decompilation: original machine code is translated into a host-native program, while a runtime layer replaces console services and graphics assumptions.

reader.standfirst: Static recompilation is becoming a practical preservation route for games whose original source is unavailable but whose executable can be analyzed systematically.
body: An emulator recreates an Xbox 360 around a game. re:Blue instead translates the game’s PowerPC code ahead of time and links it against ReXGlue, which supplies modern replacements for platform-facing behavior.
That makes host-native features possible: Linux and macOS builds, ARM64 support on those platforms, modern display modes, native input, mod loading and game-specific fixes.
The repository was pushed on August 28 and carries a 1.0.0 bump from August 27, so this is an active release rather than an abandoned proof of concept.
reader.context: The project does not distribute Blue Dragon’s commercial assets; installation verifies and extracts files from the user’s own three discs.
key_points: Recompilation translates game code once rather than emulating the CPU continuously.
A compatibility runtime becomes the replaceable boundary around the translated program.
Game-specific ports can add features that a generic emulator cannot expose cleanly.
reader.limitations: A recompilation can still inherit timing assumptions, undocumented platform behavior and game-specific edge cases; 1.0 does not mean every behavior is proven identical to original hardware.
reader.what_to_try: Read re:Blue’s build section, then inspect ReXGlue’s runtime layout to see which console assumptions are handled generically and which remain game-specific.

lead_stories.headline: A seven-star repository is preserving how discontinued Kodak/Pakon film scanners actually work
lead_stories.summary: pakon-reference documents the USB protocol, firmware loading, image stream, calibration, color pipeline and film transport of Pakon F-X35 scanners. The unusual part is its evidence discipline: claims are tied to captures, disassembly, OEM behavior, independent clients and live hardware verification, with unresolved disagreements kept explicitly unresolved.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: Hardware preservation often fails because every new driver author has to rediscover the same undocumented protocol. A neutral, provenance-marked reference can outlive any single application.

reader.standfirst: This is not a scanner app. It is an attempt to turn reverse-engineered observations into a durable public specification.
body: The project separates derived facts from copyrighted Kodak software and firmware. It publishes protocol behavior, image layout and calibration knowledge while keeping private artifacts out of the repository.

In August, a real F-135+ was driven end-to-end through an independent macOS/Linux client. That exposed facts that transmit-only captures could not prove, including reply framing, image strides and motor behavior.
The reference also compares multiple independent open-source clients and OEM binaries. Where projects disagree, the documentation records the dispute instead of forcing false certainty.
reader.context: Pakon scanners are valued by film photographers but depend on old proprietary software and hardware knowledge that was never cleanly documented for modern systems.
key_points: Protocol knowledge can be preserved independently of any driver implementation.
Confidence labels and provenance make reverse-engineered facts auditable.
Live hardware tests distinguish plausible interpretations from verified behavior.
reader.limitations: The reference is young, focused mainly on the F-135/F-135+, and some model-family behavior remains inferred or awaiting hardware confirmation.
reader.what_to_try: Open the repository’s conventions and one hardware-verified protocol page; note how confidence and source are attached to individual claims.

lead_stories.headline: Agent memory benchmarks are starting to test whether remembered evidence remains useful over time
lead_stories.summary: StreamMemBench evaluates memory systems on time-ordered life streams with paired tasks: first use observed evidence, then incorporate feedback and reuse it later. Its August 26 paper revision reports that systems often store information without reliably using it or carrying correction forward.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: A memory system can look good on retrieval tests yet fail at the actual job: turning old observations and subsequent corrections into better future behavior.

reader.standfirst: The key distinction is between possession of evidence and operational use of evidence.
body: Most memory benchmarks ask whether a fact can be recalled from a fixed history. StreamMemBench builds two-step tasks around evidence from egocentric life streams: an initial task tests evidence use, and a follow-up tests whether feedback changes later behavior.
The released benchmark contains thousands of stream segments and task pairs and compares eight memory systems across two model backbones.
The authors report a recurring failure pattern: a system may have the evidence or even absorb feedback locally, yet still fail to reuse that correction when the later task arrives.
reader.context: The benchmark is derived from EgoLife streams and is aimed at future-oriented personal assistants rather than only coding agents.
key_points: Storage, retrieval, evidence use and feedback reuse are distinct abilities.
Long-term memory should be evaluated as a trajectory, not a one-shot lookup.
A correction is only valuable if it changes later behavior.
reader.limitations: The tasks are benchmark constructions over a small number of participants and do not establish that one memory architecture will generalize to every agent workflow.
reader.what_to_try: For MAPS-style audits, record not just whether a past decision is retrieved but whether later corrections actually change the next recommendation.

lead_stories.headline: doku.md treats agent-generated Markdown as a reading problem, not another note-taking platform
lead_stories.summary: doku.md is a zero-star desktop documentation browser built around local folders, SQLite FTS5 search, file watching, tabs, bookmarks and automatic reindexing. It is explicitly aimed at projects accumulating specs, plans and task files.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: As coding agents generate more Markdown, the bottleneck can become navigation and context recovery rather than writing. A read-focused browser is a different design target from an editor or knowledge base.

reader.standfirst: The interesting idea is deliberately narrow: index a project’s documentation locally and make it fast to browse as a corpus.
body: doku.md opens a folder, scans Markdown files into SQLite FTS5, watches the filesystem for changes and reloads documents when another tool edits them.
The interface separates navigation, document reading and table of contents instead of growing into a full authoring environment.
The public repository has no stars and has not been pushed since July 6, so its value here is the mechanism and fit, not popularity or proven adoption.
reader.context: The app uses Wails, Go, Svelte and the system webview, with Linux packaging instructions in the repository.
key_points: Local full-text indexing makes generated documentation navigable without cloud ingestion.
File watching matters when agents or external editors are constantly changing the corpus.
Read-only or read-first tools can reduce interface complexity.
reader.limitations: The project is young, adoption is unclear, and promised semantic search/plugin features are not evidence of current capability.
reader.what_to_try: Point it at a documentation-heavy repository and compare context-recovery speed against browsing raw Markdown in an editor.

items.headline: ReXGlue is turning Xbox 360 recompilation into reusable infrastructure
items.summary: ReXGlue provides a runtime and toolkit for statically recompiled Xbox 360 software. re:Blue builds against it rather than carrying every compatibility mechanism inside one game project.
items.why_it_matters: A shared runtime turns one-off reverse engineering into reusable platform knowledge.
items.why_i_might_care: This is the mechanism behind a growing class of native ports from closed-console binaries.
items.limitations: Compatibility is still shaped by the games that exercise the runtime; broad platform coverage should not be assumed.

items.headline: pakon-reference treats provenance as part of the technical specification
items.summary: Each important scanner claim is tied to evidence type and confidence, with live-hardware confirmation called out separately from disassembly or inference.
items.why_it_matters: It demonstrates how to publish uncertain reverse-engineering knowledge without flattening inference into fact.
items.potential_connection: MAPS could borrow the distinction between observed, cross-confirmed, inferred and unresolved claims.

items.headline: sklauncher is a tiny terminal launcher that learns from launch history
items.summary: A Rust utility that fuzzy-searches Linux .desktop applications, executables and commands, then ranks results partly from prior launches.
items.why_it_matters: It is a narrow keyboard-first launcher that stays close to normal Linux primitives.
items.limitations: The repository was last pushed in July; it is small and not a broad desktop-search replacement.

items.headline: Interesting research: test memory as a sequence of use, correction and reuse
items.summary: StreamMemBench separates evidence recall from initial use, feedback incorporation and later reuse instead of collapsing them into one score.
items.why_it_matters: A system that stores a correction but repeats the same mistake later does not have operationally useful memory.
items.potential_connection: MAPS evaluations could include deliberate correction-follow-up pairs rather than only retrieval checks.

items.headline: Useful now: isolate parallel coding agents with Git worktrees
items.summary: Emdash gives each coding task its own Git worktree and branch, keeping filesystem changes separate until review and merge.
items.why_it_matters: This uses an existing version-control primitive as a simple sandbox for concurrent agent changes.
items.potential_connection: The mechanism is worth testing wherever MAPS allows parallel implementation work: separate mutable workspaces, shared immutable base, explicit merge point.
items.limitations: Worktree isolation prevents file collisions; it does not prevent two agents from making logically incompatible changes.

items.headline: re:Blue shows Xbox 360 recompilation becoming a consumer-facing porting method
items.summary: The project ships native builds across Windows, Linux, macOS and Steam Deck with modern rendering and mod support, while retaining a requirement for original game data.
items.why_it_matters: It demonstrates that recompilation can move beyond technical demos into installation, repair, profiles and mod workflows.

items.headline: The reusable layer matters more than any one port
items.summary: ReXGlue and earlier XenosRecomp work suggest Xbox 360 preservation is developing shared translation and runtime infrastructure rather than restarting from zero for each title.
items.why_it_matters: Shared tooling compounds reverse-engineering knowledge across games.

items.headline: doku.md: a local documentation browser for specs, plans and task files
items.summary: It indexes Markdown with SQLite FTS5, watches folders for external edits and provides a read-first three-column interface.
items.why_it_matters: It directly addresses the pile of Markdown produced by agent-heavy development workflows.

items.headline: sklauncher: fuzzy launch without installing a full desktop search layer
items.summary: It searches .desktop files, binaries and commands from a terminal UI and can bias ranking using launch history.
items.why_it_matters: A small tool can provide launcher behavior while remaining scriptable and window-manager friendly.

items.headline: A protocol reference can be the missing repair part
items.summary: pakon-reference preserves enough USB, firmware, calibration and transport behavior for modern software to keep discontinued scanners usable without treating one existing driver as the only source of truth.
items.why_it_matters: For old hardware, documentation can be as important as replacement components.

items.headline: SB Mini II rebuilds an Apple II+ around parts that are still obtainable
items.summary: A current community build replaces scarce DRAM with SRAM, omits the original composite-generation circuitry and uses a Raspberry Pi Pico to translate USB keyboard input into the Apple II keyboard matrix.
items.why_it_matters: It preserves the machine’s computational character while selectively substituting components that have become impractical to source.
items.limitations: The published how-to is explicitly still a work in progress.

items.headline: How static recompilation turns a console binary into a native PC program
items.summary: A recompiler analyzes the original executable, translates its CPU instructions ahead of time into host-callable code, then links that translated code to a compatibility runtime that supplies graphics, memory, filesystem and operating-system behavior the console used to provide.
items.why_it_matters: The expensive reverse-engineering work moves into a reusable translation/runtime layer, while each game supplies its own patches and assets.

items.headline: StreamMemBench asks whether feedback survives into the next task
items.summary: The benchmark’s paired-task design measures whether a memory system turns correction into changed future behavior rather than merely storing another note.
items.limitations: The benchmark is based on a limited set of egocentric streams and synthetic task construction around those observations.

items.headline: Scale-conditioned memory evaluation asks when irrelevant history breaks retrieval
items.summary: A separate May paper holds relevant evidence fixed while adding irrelevant sessions, then measures the point at which reliability falls below a target and how many memory calls are needed.
items.why_it_matters: ‘Works at 1,000 memories’ is incomplete unless the agent, retrieval interface, context budget and noise level are specified.
items.limitations: Results depend strongly on the tested agent and memory interface; the paper itself argues against universal scale claims.

items.headline: A 64K demo can contain its own language for choreographing hundreds of turtles
items.summary: andr00’s Revision 2026 intro uses BOGO, a custom Logo dialect, for real-time synchronization and procedural turtle choreography inside the size-constrained demoscene format.
items.why_it_matters: Extreme storage limits encourage domain-specific languages and procedural generation because instructions can be far smaller than stored media.

sections.title: You Probably Didn't Know You Were Interested In This

items.headline: Reverse-engineered documentation can be a preservation artifact in its own right
items.summary: pakon-reference is interesting even without owning a film scanner: it treats protocol facts, confidence and provenance as a durable public object separate from any implementation.
items.why_it_matters: This connects digital archives, hardware hacking and scientific reproducibility: preserve not just the program, but how we know what the machine does.

items.headline: CRDTs are what make ‘offline edits that later merge’ more than a sync slogan
items.summary: Local-first collaborative systems use conflict-free replicated data types so multiple replicas can accept edits independently and later converge without a central lockstep transaction.
items.source: A Datalog Framework for Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types
items.why_it_matters: The same mechanism sits underneath collaborative documents, offline-first apps and distributed state—two steps away from personal knowledge tools but directly relevant to resilient shared systems.

items.headline: Evidence-status labels instead of flat truth
items.summary: pakon-reference distinguishes hardware-confirmed facts, cross-confirmation, inference and unresolved disagreement.
items.potential_connection: MAPS support documents could carry claim-level authority/provenance instead of forcing every statement into the same confidence class.

items.headline: Correction-follow-up evaluation
items.summary: StreamMemBench tests whether feedback changes later behavior, not merely whether it was written to storage.
items.potential_connection: Add paired audit cases where a known correction must alter a later recommendation or handoff.

items.headline: Worktree isolation for parallel mutable work
items.summary: Emdash assigns concurrent coding tasks separate Git worktrees and branches, then reunifies them through explicit review and merge.
items.potential_connection: A cheap sandbox boundary for parallel agents: isolate changes physically, compare diffs, merge only reviewed state.

rabbit_hole.headline: Trace Blue Dragon from Xbox 360 binary to native PC runtime
rabbit_hole.summary: Start with re:Blue’s README, then open ReXGlue and identify which pieces are game code translation versus reusable console-runtime replacement. The distinction is the core mechanism behind this new wave of ports.
